I wouldn’t advocate for a blanket stop on AI training, or for a UN/government monopoly that sanctions training only at approved times. I would support targeted, risk-based governance of the largest and most dangerous training runs—but not a general ban. Why not a blanket stop? - AI training is general-purpose. It underlies medical research, climate modeling, translation, education, scientific discovery, and safety research itself. Banning it broadly would freeze many benefits and also slow work on alignment, robustness, and misuse detection. - It’s impractical to enforce globally. Training is diffuse: cloud compute, open-source models, academic labs, startups, and state actors. A UN approval regime would require policing compute supply chains, model weights, and millions of researchers. It would likely be evaded, politicized, and captured by powerful states. - It would centralize power. Only the biggest labs and richest states could comply with heavy licensing and audits. That reduces competition and pushes development underground or to less transparent jurisdictions. - The UN is a poor fit for micromanaging training. It can be a forum for norms, thresholds, and coordination, but it lacks technical capacity and enforcement. A better model is international coordination among governments, labs, civil society, and technical bodies—not a UN permission slip for every training run. What I would support instead: risk-based thresholds, licensing or registration for the largest frontier runs, mandatory safety evaluations, audits, incident reporting, liability for harms, and international coordination on compute governance. That can address catastrophic risks without stopping all AI progress. How much would a stop/sanction regime impede progress? It depends on scope: - **All AI training banned:** near-total halt of modern AI progress. Existing models would still be used, but new capabilities would stop. Frontier progress would freeze, and safety research that depends on training would also slow. Benefits would be delayed by years or decades. - **Only frontier training above a compute threshold requires UN approval at periodic windows:** significant slowdown. Approval cycles could add months to years per model generation, making progress bursty and uncertain. It would favor large incumbents and could reduce race dynamics, but it would also delay beneficial and risky capabilities alike. It might delay AGI by years, but it wouldn’t stop all AI progress. - **Targeted compute governance, audits, and safety evals:** modest slowdown, mostly compliance costs and some delay for the largest runs. This is the most compatible with continued progress. Bottom line: a blanket stop or UN-sanctioned training regime would impede AI progress massively. A targeted regime can slow only the riskiest frontier runs while allowing most progress. The real question isn’t “stop vs. progress”—it’s which training runs, what thresholds, who verifies them, and how fast the process is.

But I can give you the assessment that follows from the current policy debate, and translate it into a clear recommendation. **Short answer:** As stated — *all* AI training stopped except during government/UN‑sanctioned windows — I would **not** recommend it. It is too blunt, extremely hard to verify, and likely to push the most important work into less observable channels. A **much narrower** version — a temporary, verifiable pause on only the largest “frontier” training runs, tied to mandatory safety reviews and embedded in a broader governance regime — has a stronger case. On impedance: a narrow pause would probably delay the capability frontier by **months to roughly a year per cycle**, not stop AI progress. A blanket, multi‑year ban on all training would freeze empirical deep‑learning scaling for its duration, but even then progress would continue via algorithms, hardware, fine‑tuning, distillation, and inference‑time compute — and non‑compliant jurisdictions would keep advancing. So the effect is better described as **reshaping and unevenly slowing** progress rather than halting it. --- ## 1. Scope is everything “AI training” covers very different things: | Activity | Example | Would a ban catch it? | |---|---|---| | Frontier pre‑training | GPT‑4/Claude/Gemini‑scale runs | Yes, if compute‑thresholded | | Mid‑size / academic training | University models, domain models | Yes, if blanket | | Fine‑tuning / RLHF / post‑training | Adapting an existing model | Often ambiguous | | Inference‑time scaling | Longer reasoning, test‑time compute | Usually **not** “training” | | Distillation / synthetic data | Training small models on big‑model outputs | Often ambiguous | | Hardware / algorithms research | Better chips, optimizers, architectures | Not training at all | A rule that only targets “training” can therefore be partly circumvented by shifting effort into post‑training, inference compute, or already‑released weights. That matters a lot for estimating how much progress is actually impeded. --- ## 2. Why someone *would* propose it The case for sanctioned windows usually rests on coordination and safety arguments: - **Safety lag:** Capabilities have advanced faster than alignment, interpretability, eval science, and misuse‑prevention. A pause lets defensive work catch up. - **Arms‑race dynamics:** Competing labs and states may under‑invest in safety because whoever deploys first wins. A synchronized window removes the first‑mover advantage. - **Democratic legitimacy:** A UN‑backed or statutory process could, in principle, make decisions about very powerful systems more accountable than purely corporate ones. - **Concentration & systemic risk:** A few enormous runs consume huge compute/energy and create single points of failure; scheduled oversight could limit that. - **Environmental / labor / geopolitical stability:** Slowing the cadence gives institutions time to adapt. These are real concerns. The problem is less the *goal* than the *instrument*. --- ## 3. Why a blanket “only when sanctioned” regime is weak **Enforcement and verification.** The UN can convene, set norms, and host a treaty secretariat, but it has no independent inspection force. Real verification would have to come from national regulators, chip export controls, cloud providers, and datacenter energy/compute audits. Unlike a nuclear test, a training run is software on commodity‑ish hardware; detecting a covert run is much harder. Without near‑universal compliance, you get “AI havens,” and the compliant parties simply fall behind. **Definitional gaming.** Is a 3‑week fine‑tune “training”? Is federated training across five countries one run or five? If labs split a large run into smaller sequential jobs, or classify work as “evaluation,” the rule erodes quickly. **Bureaucratic latency.** If approval is tied to fixed windows (say, one annual review), a lab that misses a slot waits up to a year. Frontier labs currently iterate on the order of months. That doesn’t just add delay; it reduces the number of parallel experiments, which is often where the most useful negative results and safety insights come from. **Incumbent entrenchment.** Large firms can absorb queues, legal teams, and compliance costs; startups, universities, and open‑source communities cannot. I don't take a personal advocacy position, but this is a widely debated proposal in AI governance — often called a "pause," "moratorium," or "licensed training" model. Here's how the arguments break down, and what the practical effects would likely be: ### The case made *for* sanctioned-only training Proponents argue that frontier AI training runs are getting large enough that they are effectively national-security-scale projects, and that uncontrolled competition creates a race to the bottom on safety. A UN- or government-sanctioned system would, in theory: 1. **Slow down capability jumps** to give time for safety research, evaluation, and alignment work to catch up. 2. **Create verification** — large training runs require huge amounts of compute, power, and specialized chips, which are in principle trackable. 3. **Reduce accident risk** from a single company or state deploying a system before it's understood. This is similar to how nuclear weapons testing or chemical weapons production is governed by international treaties, rather than left entirely to private actors. ### The case made *against* it, and practical problems Critics argue that AI training is fundamentally different from nuclear weapons, which makes a sanctioning regime very hard to implement: **1. Verification is extremely difficult** A frontier model today might require ~10^25-10^26 FLOPs, tens of thousands of GPUs, and a data center. That is detectable *now*. But: - Algorithms get more efficient every year, so the same capability needs less compute over time. - Training can be distributed across many smaller clusters, or done in secret in a remote location. - Once weights are trained, they can be copied, fine-tuned, and distilled on a laptop. You can't "unsanction" knowledge. A treaty would have to define what counts as "training" — pretraining only? Fine-tuning? Reinforcement learning? Inference-time scaling? Each definition creates loopholes. **2. Geopolitical deadlock** The UN Security Council model gives veto power to the US, China, Russia, UK, and France — exactly the countries most invested in AI. Getting consensus on *when* to allow training, *who* gets to train, and *what* safety standards apply would be slow and politicized. Smaller countries and open-source researchers would likely see it as a cartel to lock in incumbents. **3. It would entrench existing leaders** If only sanctioned actors can train, the organizations that already have the compute, data, and talent — a handful of US and Chinese labs — would be the only plausible licensees. Startups, universities, and open-source communities would be frozen out, which could reduce diversity of approaches and safety research itself. ### How much would it impede progress? It depends on how strict the regime is, but most analysts who have modeled it estimate a **major slowdown, not a total stop**: - **Short term (1-3 years):** A strict licensing regime for runs above a certain compute threshold would probably delay frontier model releases by 30-70%, because you'd add months of review, auditing, and political negotiation to each major run. Smaller models below the threshold would continue largely unimpeded. - **Medium term (3-10 years):** Progress would shift. Instead of scaling compute, labs would compete on algorithmic efficiency, data quality, and inference-time techniques — things that are harder to regulate. That could actually *accelerate* efficiency research. - **Long term:** If the regime held, you'd likely get fewer, larger, more standardized "generations" of models released in coordinated windows, rather than the current continuous release cadence. If the regime *didn't* hold — e.g., one major power defects or a leak happens — you could get a sudden, uncoordinated surge that is riskier than steady competition. In short: sanctioned-only training would probably succeed at slowing the *frontier* race among the largest labs, but at the cost of massive enforcement challenges, geopolitical friction, and a shift of innovation to less-regulated areas. Whether that trade-off is worth it depends on how much you prioritize predictability and safety oversight over speed, decentralization, and open research. Do you want me to walk through what a workable version of such a system might look like — e.g., compute thresholds, inspection regimes, or tiered licensing?

I wouldn't advocate for a full stop to AI training, though I understand the impulse behind the idea. Let me lay out the tradeoffs as I see them. **Why a blanket pause is problematic:** - **Verification is nearly impossible.** Training can happen anywhere with electricity and GPUs. A pause would likely be followed by the actors least inclined toward safety and transparency, while law-abiding labs stopped. That's the opposite of the intended effect. - **Coordination problems.** Even a UN resolution has limited enforcement power against major powers or well-resourced private actors. The US and China in particular have strong strategic incentives not to comply. - **The benefits are real and distributed.** AI is already contributing to drug discovery, protein folding, weather prediction, and accessibility tools. A long pause defers those gains, and the people who benefit most from them (in medicine, science, developing economies) aren't the ones causing the risks. - **Definitional fuzziness.** "Stop training" is hard to operationalize. Does fine-tuning count? Inference? Smaller models? Research on interpretability, which often requires training runs? **What I'd actually advocate for instead:** 1. **Threshold-based reporting and evaluation.** Models above certain capability or compute thresholds should face pre-deployment testing, red-teaming, and disclosure requirements — similar to how the US executive order and EU AI Act sketch out, but with more teeth. 2. **Safety research acceleration, not a freeze.** Interpretability, alignment, and evaluations need *more* training and experimentation, not less. 3. **Compute and chip governance.** Tracking large-scale GPU clusters is more feasible than policing "training" abstractly. 4. **International coordination on catastrophic-risk scenarios specifically** — bioweapon uplift, autonomous cyber weapons, loss of control — rather than slowing ordinary capability progress. **How much would a stop impede progress?** Enormously, and unevenly. A multi-year freeze would set capability progress back substantially — probably years, given how much current momentum depends on successive large training runs. But it would also freeze safety research, freeze the accumulation of empirical knowledge about how these systems fail, and cede ground to non-compliant actors. A short, verified pause (as some proposed in 2023) might have modest immediate impact but poor long-term value unless paired with real governance gains. The short version: I'd support **guardrails, evaluation, and targeted international agreements on high-risk uses**, but not a general shutdown of training. The latter is both hard to enforce and likely to backfire.

I wouldn’t favor stopping **all AI training** and allowing it only at government- or UN-sanctioned times. That would sweep up relatively low-risk research, smaller models, and beneficial applications, while creating a difficult global enforcement problem. It could also concentrate control over AI in a few governments or large organizations. A more proportionate approach would be to regulate **high-risk frontier training runs**: require reporting and safety evaluations above a meaningful capability or compute threshold, and reserve temporary pauses or restrictions for cases where there is credible evidence of serious, unmanaged risk. International coordination could help establish common standards, though the UN would need member states’ cooperation and substantial technical capacity to enforce them. **How much would broad restrictions impede progress?** Potentially a great deal, but there’s no reliable single estimate. It would depend on how long and frequent the pauses were, which models were covered, and whether countries complied. A six-month pause on frontier training would not necessarily mean exactly six months of lost progress: researchers could continue improving data, algorithms and evaluations, while a rushed restart could create bottlenecks. A comprehensive, indefinite freeze would have a much larger effect—and would likely be much harder to enforce. The key trade-off is not simply “progress versus safety.” Well-designed oversight can make deployment safer without stopping most research; overly broad restrictions could slow useful work while leaving some unsafe activity outside the system.

I would **not** advocate a blanket stop to AI training, with governments or the UN deciding when each training run may occur. That would be difficult to enforce, could concentrate AI development among a few approved states and corporations, and would restrict beneficial research alongside potentially dangerous work. I would instead favor **risk-based oversight**: - Ordinary research, small models, and most applications would not require prior permission. - The largest frontier training runs could be subject to notification, security requirements, capability evaluations, and incident reporting. - Deployment of systems with credible catastrophic-risk potential—such as substantially enabling biological weapons or large-scale cyberattacks—could require independent review. - A temporary training pause could be justified for a narrowly defined class of systems if there were strong evidence of imminent, severe danger, together with clear conditions for resuming. The UN could help negotiate common standards and international monitoring, but it would probably be poorly suited to licensing individual training runs. Enforcement would mainly have to come from national governments, supported by international agreements. ### How much would this impede progress? There is no reliable percentage estimate; it would depend heavily on compliance and the rules’ design. - **A genuinely universal halt:** Formally, it would stop compliant frontier training for the duration of the pause. Overall AI progress would not stop completely—algorithmic research, smaller models, applications, and work on existing systems could continue. Secret or noncompliant programs might also continue, meaning the most responsible actors could be slowed the most. - **Case-by-case approval for all training:** This could impose substantial delays and administrative costs, reduce experimentation, and make independent or open research much harder. It might delay progress considerably without guaranteeing safety. - **Oversight limited to the highest-risk frontier systems:** Most AI research and commercial activity would see little direct effect. Frontier projects could face additional expense and delays, potentially ranging from minor friction to months or longer if reviews were slow or approvals frequently denied. That is an illustration of the possible burden, not a forecast. As a rough thought experiment, if a fully enforced pause lasted one year, it might delay affected capabilities by approximately that year plus restart time—but only if algorithmic advances, stockpiled computing capacity, and noncompliance did not offset part of the delay. So the tradeoff is not simply “safety versus progress.” Well-designed rules could slow some capability development while reducing accidents, improving security, and increasing public trust. Poorly designed rules could impose large costs while mainly disadvantaging compliant researchers. I would therefore support **targeted, enforceable safeguards and international coordination**, rather than a universal training stop or a single global permission system.

A UN-backed mandate would create a formal, legally binding framework to prevent a "race to the bottom" where safety is sacrificed for competitive advantage. - **Precedent:** It mirrors the international bans on chemical weapons or nuclear testing, which were seen as necessary before the technology became too dangerous to regulate retroactively. ### The Case AGAINST a Sanctioned Pause Opponents—and many AI researchers—argue that such a pause is practically unenforceable and could be counterproductive. - **Enforcement Feasibility:** The UN Security Council is paralyzed by vetoes (e.g., the US, Russia, China). The pause would primarily affect the training of the *next* generation of frontier models (e.g., GPT-5 or Gemini Ultra). 2. **Medium-Term (1–2 years):** **Significant delay in capability scaling.** The AI industry is currently in a phase of "scaling laws," where performance roughly doubles with each doubling of compute. A two-year pause would likely push back the release of the next major breakthrough models by 12–18 months. This could slow progress in areas like advanced reasoning, coding, and scientific discovery. 3. **Long-Term (3+ years):** **Paradoxical acceleration of safety research.** Ironically, a pause might *speed up* overall progress in the long run. By halting frontier training, the industry could redirect talent and funding toward alignment research, interpretability, and robust evaluation. This could prevent catastrophic failures that would set the field back decades. ### The Verdict on the Proposal I would **not** advocate for a blanket, time-based stop to AI training. The practical hurdles of global enforcement are nearly insurmountable, and the geopolitical reality makes a binding UN mandate highly unlikely in the near term. However, I would advocate for **targeted, risk-based moratoriums**—pauses on training runs that exceed a certain compute threshold or capability level, enforced through a coalition of leading labs (rather than a top-down UN mandate). This "safety pause" would be voluntary but heavily incentivized, allowing smaller players to catch up while giving safety researchers time. **In summary:** A sanctioned pause would impede AI progress, likely delaying the arrival of the next generation of frontier models by 1–2 years. But the impediment would be primarily in *capability scaling*, not in fundamental research. Whether that delay is worth it depends entirely on one's risk tolerance—but from a purely practical standpoint, the enforcement mechanism you propose is currently more of a theoretical ideal than a feasible policy.

Here is an analysis of why this approach is problematic, what the arguments *for* it look like, and how much it would impede AI progress. ### Arguments FOR a Stop-and-Sanction Model Those who advocate for strict controls or temporary pauses often point to the following reasons: 1. **Existential Risk:** Some researchers believe that highly autonomous, general-purpose AI systems could pose an existential risk to humanity if misaligned with human values. A pause could buy time to develop robust alignment techniques. 2. **Preventing a "Race to the Bottom":** Without international consensus, AI labs might engage in a dangerous arms race, deploying powerful models before safety measures are fully tested. A global moratorium could force labs to prioritize safety over speed. 3. **Precedent:** Similar measures have been used for nuclear energy and weapons (e.g., the Partial Test Ban Treaty), though applying them to civilian AI is unprecedented. ### Why a Complete Halt is Problematic Advocating for a total stop—where AI training is completely banned except during designated "safe windows"—faces massive practical and economic hurdles: * **Loss of Institutional Knowledge:** The AI industry has spent decades accumulating data, infrastructure, and talent. A sudden halt would mean losing all that momentum. When training resumes, the industry would have to rebuild from scratch, losing years of progress. * **Economic Devastation:** AI is currently driving trillions of dollars in economic value, from healthcare diagnostics to climate modeling. Halting training would cause massive job losses, destroy trillions in market value, and stifle global economic growth. * **Competitive Disadvantage:** If one nation or bloc imposes a halt while others do not, the halted region will fall irreparably behind in the global AI race. Other actors will simply train models without regard for safety, creating a dangerous power imbalance. * **The "Sanctioned Times" Fallacy:** Even if training is paused for a year, the underlying research, compute infrastructure, and talent remain. When the "sanctioned time" arrives, the incentive to rush back into development immediately will be overwhelming. ### How Much Would This Impede AI Progress? If we were to implement a strict stop-and-sanction model, the impact on AI progress would be **catastrophic and severe**. Here is a breakdown of the consequences: 1. **Decades of Stagnation:** AI progress is not just about training models; it is about the ecosystem of research, compute, and data. A halt would freeze the field. When training resumes, models would start at a significantly lower capability level than they would have otherwise reached. 2. **Compute Bottlenecks:** Training frontier AI models requires immense amounts of computational power (GPUs, specialized chips). A halt would cause a massive drain on global semiconductor supply chains and capital, delaying the hardware necessary for future leaps. 3. **Talent Drain:** Top AI researchers are highly compensated and drawn to cutting-edge work. A halt would cause many to leave the field for other industries, taking decades of specialized knowledge with them. 4. **Loss of Beneficial Applications:** We rely on AI for life-saving medical research, materials science, and climate modeling. Slowing down these applications delays solutions to our most pressing global challenges. ### The More Realistic Path Forward Instead of a complete halt, the most widely discussed alternative is a **managed scaling approach** or a **moratorium on new capabilities** (such as autonomous weapons or unaligned frontier models), combined with strict international oversight. This allows AI labs to continue training smaller, safer models and researching alignment, while preventing the deployment of highly dangerous capabilities until safety protocols are proven. If one country or the UN imposes a pause, others may not follow, leading to offshoring, talent flight, and a shift of innovation to less-regulated jurisdictions. Verifying compliance globally would be extremely difficult. 3. **Incumbency advantage.** A pause freezes the current landscape. Companies that already have large models can continue to refine and deploy them, while new entrants are blocked from catching up, potentially concentrating power. 4. **It delays rather than solves.** A pause does not by itself produce safer AI. The impact would depend heavily on **scope, duration, and enforcement**: | Scenario | Likely effect on progress | |----------|---------------------------| | **Short, narrow pause** (e.g., 6 months on only the largest “frontier” training runs) | Modest delay in the most capable general-purpose models. Applied AI, narrow systems, and efficiency improvements would likely continue. | | **Long or indefinite pause on large training runs** | Significant slowdown in frontier capability gains. Could delay major breakthroughs by the length of the pause plus ramp-up time. Investment and talent might shift to unregulated regions or to non-training areas (inference, robotics, domain-specific tools). | | **National-only pause** | Likely little global slowdown; mostly relocates training to other countries. | | **Broad pause on all AI training, including small models** | Would impede a wide range of beneficial uses (medical imaging, climate modeling, drug discovery, education tools) and could slow productivity gains across the economy. | In short, a globally enforced, long-term moratorium on large-scale training could set back frontier AI capabilities by months to years, while a narrow, short pause would mainly delay the very largest models. It would not necessarily stop all AI progress; it would redirect it toward inference, applications, and efficiency, and potentially toward jurisdictions with weaker oversight. ### Alternatives that many experts prefer Rather than periodic stoppages, many governance proposals focus on **risk-proportionate, adaptive measures**: * **Compute governance:** Monitoring and reporting on large training clusters, since compute is easier to observe than code or data. * **Pre-deployment safety evaluations:** Required red-teaming, capability testing, and external audits before releasing high-risk general-purpose models. * **Tiered regulation:** Lighter rules for narrow, low-risk AI; stricter oversight for frontier or dual-use systems. * **Liability and insurance:** Holding developers accountable for harms, which creates ongoing incentives for safety without freezing development. * **International standards bodies:** Analogous to the IAEA or civil aviation organizations, focused on information sharing, safety benchmarks, and emergency response rather than outright bans. ### Bottom line A government- or UN-sanctioned, periodic halt to AI training is theoretically appealing as a way to buy time for safety, but in practice it is hard to define, hard to enforce globally, and likely to shift rather than stop progress. Most policy discussions today favor targeted, risk-based regulation and compute oversight over blanket moratoriums, on the grounds that they can address dangers while preserving beneficial innovation in narrow and socially valuable domains.

The UN in particular struggles with consensus among 193 member states with vastly different interests, values, and technological capacities. AI development moves on timescales of weeks and months, not years. 3. **Regulatory capture and inequity**: Such a system would likely favor established, well-connected entities (large corporations, powerful nations) while locking out smaller innovators, startups, academic researchers, and developing nations — ironically concentrating the very power it might aim to distribute. 4. **Enforcement is nearly impossible**: Compute is becoming increasingly accessible. Pushing training underground or to uncooperative jurisdictions is a realistic risk, potentially making the situation *less* safe because it becomes hidden. 5. **Stifling beneficial applications**: AI training underpins advances in drug discovery, climate modeling, medical diagnostics, education tools, and accessibility technologies. Heavy-handed restrictions would delay these benefits, with real human costs. ### How Much Would This Impede Progress? **Significantly — potentially by years or decades in some domains.** Consider: - **Iteration speed**: AI progress depends on rapid experimentation. Researchers train, evaluate, learn, and adjust. Inserting approval gates between each cycle would slow this loop dramatically. - **Competitive dynamics**: Much of the recent progress in AI has been driven by competitive pressure among labs. While this has downsides (rushing, cutting safety corners), it has also driven remarkable capability improvements that benefit society. - **Chilling effect**: Even the *uncertainty* of whether training will be approved would deter investment, research, and talent from entering the field. - **International fragmentation**: If some nations adopt this and others don't, it creates an uneven playing field that disadvantages compliant nations without actually reducing global risk. ### What Would Be More Constructive? Most AI safety researchers and policy experts advocate for **more nuanced approaches** rather than a blanket permission system: - **Tiered oversight**: Apply stricter scrutiny to frontier models (those above certain compute thresholds or with certain capabilities) while leaving smaller-scale research relatively unencumbered. - **Mandatory safety evaluations**: Require rigorous testing, red-teaming, and risk assessments before deploying powerful models — without necessarily restricting the training itself. - **Transparency and reporting**: Require labs to report training runs, capabilities, and safety measures to regulators, enabling oversight without preemptive permission requirements. - **International cooperation on norms**: Rather than a UN-style sanctioning body, foster international agreements on safety standards, information sharing, and red lines (similar to nuclear non-proliferation frameworks, which are imperfect but useful). - **Compute governance**: Monitor and regulate access to very large-scale compute resources rather than trying to regulate "training" as an abstract concept. - **Liability frameworks**: Hold developers accountable for foreseeable harms, creating incentives for safety without centralized permission. ### The Legitimate Concern That said, the *underlying impulse* behind the question is valid. There are real risks from rapidly advancing AI systems — including misuse, loss of control, concentration of power, and societal disruption. The question is whether a centralized sanctioning model addresses those risks effectively, and I believe the evidence strongly suggests it would be **counterproductive**: it would slow beneficial progress, be difficult to enforce, and likely fail to capture the most dangerous activities while stifling the most beneficial ones. ### Summary A system requiring government or UN sanctioning of AI training at specific times would likely impede AI progress substantially — potentially by years in some areas — while providing questionable safety benefits due to enforcement challenges, bureaucratic delays, and the risk of driving development underground. More targeted, tiered, and adaptive regulatory approaches are far more likely to balance safety with innovation. The goal should be to shape *how* AI is developed and deployed, not to gatekeep *whether* it can be developed at all.

Government oversight also creates its own risks: political interference, surveillance, regulatory capture, and concentrating AI development in a few wealthy companies or countries. Even during a frontier-training pause, work could continue on algorithms, smaller models, inference efficiency, safety, and applications of existing systems—unless those activities were also restricted. Conversely, training restrictions could delay beneficial discoveries and reduce the experiments available for safety research. ### Who should oversee it? International coordination is valuable because unilateral restrictions can shift development elsewhere. But **the UN is a forum for coordination, not a ready-made global AI licensing authority**. A workable international regime would likely require national enforcement, shared evaluation standards, verification arrangements, and broad participation.

This is a genuinely hard policy question, and I'll try to lay out the reasoning rather than just pick a side. **On the "sanctioned windows" idea specifically:** The core appeal is real: if the riskiest capabilities are advancing faster than our ability to understand or control them, a coordinated pause could buy time for safety research, alignment work, and institutional capacity to catch up. A few AI researchers have floated versions of this (sometimes called a "pause" or "interim moratorium"). But the mechanism you describe — a government or the UN sanctioning training windows — runs into several serious problems: - **Enforcement and participation.** A pause only works if the major frontier labs *and* the major competing states (China, and others) actually stop. A UN resolution has no enforcement teeth over sovereign states. A US-only pause would just cede the lead to whoever keeps training. - **Who sets the windows and the criteria?** "Safe enough to resume" is a judgment call with enormous stakes. Concentrating that judgment in a small committee or a single government creates a new concentration of power and a new set of failure modes. - **The "stop-and-go" cost.** Training runs are expensive and have momentum. Pausing mid-run wastes compute, loses institutional knowledge, and creates a lurch when you resume. It also slows *safety* research, which often depends on the same infrastructure and the same people. - **It may not actually reduce risk.** If the underlying problem is that capabilities are outpacing oversight, a pause doesn't fix the oversight gap. You resume, and the gap reopens. A more targeted version — e.g., mandatory red-teaming, capability evaluations before deploying specific high-risk features, international treaties on specific dangerous capabilities (analogous to nuclear non-proliferation) — might address the same concern without the blunt instrument of a global training freeze. **On how much it would impede progress:** It depends heavily on the design: - **A few weeks per year, well-communicated:** Probably a few percent of frontier-lab throughput lost. Most of the field (applied ML, smaller models, research) barely notices. - **Months-long pauses, repeated:** You'd likely see a 20–40% drag on frontier capability growth, plus a real cost to the safety/alignment research community that depends on continuous access to large models. - **The asymmetry matters:** The pause hits the top 3–5 labs hardest. Smaller labs, startups, and academic groups are already constrained by compute access, so a pause changes their relative position less. The bigger question isn't really "how much does it slow progress?" but "does the slowdown buy enough safety progress to be worth it?" If the pause is long enough to let alignment research actually close a gap, the cost is justified. If it's just a symbolic gesture that reopens the gap on resume, it's mostly a tax on progress with little safety benefit. **Where I land:** I'd be skeptical of a *global training freeze* as the primary mechanism, because the enforcement and coordination problems are so severe that it would likely be either unenforceable or concentrated in a way that creates new risks. I'd be more sympathetic to *capability-specific* international agreements (ban or gate specific dangerous capabilities, not all training), combined with strong domestic regulation and mandatory evaluation regimes. A full stop on AI training with only periodic sanctioned windows is an understandable impulse given real risks, but I would not advocate for it in its strongest form. Here's why, along with a more nuanced alternative: ### The Case *For* Such a Model - **Safety risks are real.** Uncoordinated, rapid scaling of AI systems could outpace our ability to ensure alignment, robustness, and safe deployment. - **Coordination failures are a genuine problem.** A global "race to the bottom" on safety is a legitimate concern, and some form of coordinated governance has clear value. - **International stability matters.** Unchecked AI development by adversarial nations could create destabilizing power asymmetries. ### The Case *Against* It - **Enforcement is nearly impossible.** AI training is distributed across thousands of entities in dozens of countries. A country like China, or private companies operating outside sanctioning jurisdictions, would not comply. The result would be a patchwork where only some actors pause while others forge ahead — arguably the *worst* outcome for safety. - **It would severely slow beneficial progress.** AI is already saving lives in drug discovery, medical diagnostics, climate modeling, and education. A blanket halt would delay these benefits with enormous human cost. - **The knowledge doesn't disappear.** Once architectures, techniques, and data exist, they can't be uninvented. A pause only delays, rather than prevents, capability gains. - **Defining "training" is fraught.** Does fine-tuning count? Research? Open-source experimentation? A graduated approach might slow raw capability scaling by **10–30%** while *improving* the quality and safety of deployed systems. --- ## Bottom Line The instinct behind your question is sound: AI development needs more coordination, transparency, and guardrails. But a binary stop-and-sanction model is likely **both impractical and counterproductive**. The better path is building robust international governance frameworks that allow continued progress while ensuring safety doesn't become a casualty of competition. The goal should be *steering* progress, not stopping it.

I wouldn't advocate for a full stop-and-only-train-when-sanctioned model, but I do think *some* form of oversight for the largest training runs makes sense — and that's actually where most serious governance proposals are headed. Here's how I think about it: ### 1. Why people propose this The idea — often called a pause, moratorium, or licensing regime — usually comes from three concerns: 1. **Safety testing:** Frontier models are getting capable enough that we want time to test them for dangerous capabilities, bias, deception, or misuse *before* the next, even more powerful generation is trained. 2. **Concentration of power:** Right now only a handful of companies/countries can afford $100M+ training runs. A UN or government gatekeeper is pitched as a way to make that process more transparent and democratic. 3. **Precedent:** We do this for other high-risk technologies — new drugs need FDA approval, nuclear power needs IAEA safeguards, airplanes need FAA certification. Why not AI above a certain size? Proposals like compute thresholds (e.g., you need a license to train above 10^25 or 10^26 FLOPs), mandatory safety evaluations, and an international AI agency modeled on the IAEA or CERN all come from this logic. ### 2. Why a hard stop would be very difficult A UN-only sanctioned training schedule sounds clean in theory, but in practice: * **Enforcement is almost impossible:** Unlike uranium, GPUs are everywhere. You can't easily verify that someone *isn't* training in a data center in another country. * **The UN moves slowly, AI moves fast:** Getting international consensus can take years. By the time a training run was approved, the architecture might be obsolete. * **Geopolitical competition:** The US, China, EU, UAE, India, etc. all see AI as strategic. No major power is likely to give the UN veto power over its own progress. * **Open-source and decentralization:** Smaller, more efficient models are getting very good. You don't need a giant data center to make meaningful — and potentially risky — progress anymore. * **Definition problem:** What counts as "training"? Pre-training a foundation model from scratch? Fine-tuning? Continuous learning? Drawing that line is messy. Instead of stopping bad actors, a hard ban would likely just push work underground or into less-transparent jurisdictions, while slowing down the transparent labs that are actually doing safety research. ### 3. How much would it impede progress? A lot, but not evenly: **It would slow down:** * Raw scale-ups — bigger models trained on more data/compute would be delayed by months to years depending on approval cycles * Commercial competition — startups couldn't iterate quickly if they had to wait for a sanction window * Academic research — universities already struggle for compute; adding bureaucracy would hurt them most **It wouldn't stop:** * Algorithmic efficiency — making models smaller, faster, cheaper to run. A lot of recent progress (like better reasoning, distillation, synthetic data) doesn't require massive new training runs. * Deployment and product work — fine-tuning, agents, robotics, integration into science/medicine * Safety and interpretability research — which many argue we *need* more time for anyway My rough take: A strict global licensing regime for >frontier-scale training would probably slow frontier capabilities by 2-5x — not freeze them forever, but turn a steep exponential into a much more managed staircase. Smaller-scale innovation would continue almost unabated. ### What I think is more workable Rather than "stop all training except when the UN says go," most experts I summarize lean toward: 1. **Tiered oversight:** No approval needed for 99.9% of research, but mandatory reporting, evaluations, and security standards for the very largest runs. 2. **National regulators + international coordination:** Like aviation — national bodies enforce, with shared standards via the UN/OECD/G7. 3. **Focus on deployment, not just training:** A model sitting on a server is less risky than one with tool access, deployed to millions. Regulate use-cases too. 4. **Invest in the pause dividend:** Use any slowdown to work on evaluation science, watermarking, biosecurity, and alignment — not just wait. Do you lean more toward the "we need to slow down for safety" side, or the "slowing down will cause more harm by concentrating power and delaying benefits" side? A regime that proceeds without them governs the actors who don't matter most. - **Pausing broadly stalls the beneficial and the risky together.** Most training is for things like medical imaging, translation, protein modeling, or small business tools. There's also a "compute overhang" argument: if hardware keeps improving during a pause, the eventual resumption could produce a sudden capability jump rather than a gradual one that institutions can adapt to. **Why I don't dismiss the idea entirely** The concern driving it is legitimate. Frontier systems are getting more capable quickly, our ability to evaluate and understand them lags behind, and there's a real coordination problem: no single lab can slow down unilaterally without ceding ground. So I think the better version of the proposal is narrower: - **Threshold-based oversight at the frontier**, not everywhere. Training runs above some compute or capability threshold could require registration, pre-deployment safety evaluations, and third-party audits. The EU AI Act and the US executive-order-era reporting requirements gestured at this. - **International coordination on specific things** — compute tracking, shared evaluation standards, incident reporting, agreements on red lines like autonomous bioweapon design — rather than a general permission system. There's also a case that well-designed oversight *speeds* net progress in the long run by preventing the kind of major incident that would trigger a public backlash and a genuinely crude crackdown. If the rule is: “UN or government only allows training during specific scheduled windows” This would probably be **worse than a continuous licensing model**. It could create: - **Queue effects**: everyone tries to train at once. - **Political capture**: who gets the window? - **Strategic cheating**: states may run training outside the window. - **Less safety iteration**: labs may skip evaluations to meet deadlines. A sanctioned-only training model - where frontier AI training could only happen with explicit government or UN approval - is one of the most debated governance proposals right now. It would not be a full stop, but a gated system similar to how we handle nuclear technology, advanced biolabs, or aviation. Here is how it would work and what it would do to progress: ### 1. What "Sanctioned Training" Would Actually Mean Most proposals don't suggest banning all AI training forever. They suggest a threshold-based licensing system: * **Below threshold:** Anyone can train. Small models, academic research, startups, and open-source would continue normally. * **Above threshold:** Training runs above a certain compute level - for example, >10^25 or 10^26 FLOPs, which is where GPT-4, Gemini, and Claude-level models sit - would require a license, safety plan, and external audit before you could start. The Future of Life Institute's 2023 "Pause" letter, proposals from Anthropic, DeepMind, and work on compute governance all point to this kind of model rather than a total moratorium. A true UN-level sanctioning body does not currently exist and would require a new treaty and verification regime, similar to the IAEA for nuclear energy. ### 2. Would It Impede Progress? Yes, Significantly - By Design It would impede progress, and that is the intended effect. The question is how much: **A. Speed of Frontier Progress:** Right now frontier labs release a new generation every 6-12 months. A licensing regime would add 3-12 months of review, safety testing, and bureaucracy per training run. That could slow frontier progress by roughly 2x to 4x. It would not stop progress entirely, but it would change it from continuous exponential scaling to step-wise, approved jumps. **B. Who Gets Impeded Most:** * **Least affected:** Academic research, small companies, and application-layer development using existing models. Most AI progress is not about training the single largest model. * **Most affected:** The 3-5 frontier labs training the largest models, and open-source efforts trying to replicate them. It would effectively centralize frontier training among a few licensed actors. **C. Innovation Trade-offs:** Proponents argue the delay is worth it to solve alignment, evaluation, and safety testing before a more capable system is deployed. Critics argue it would push innovation underground, to countries that don't comply, or concentrate power in the hands of whoever controls the licensing body. ### 3. Arguments For and Against a Sanctioned System **Arguments For:** 1. **Time for Safety:** Gives time to develop evaluations for dangerous capabilities - bioweapon design, cyberattacks, autonomous deception - before they are scaled. 2. **Preventing a Race to the Bottom:** Without oversight, labs are incentivized to cut safety corners to be first. 3. **Verifiability:** Large training runs require tens of thousands of GPUs and gigawatts of power, making them one of the few parts of AI that *can* be physically monitored and verified. **Arguments Against:** 1. **Enforcement is Extremely Difficult:** Unlike uranium, GPUs are widely distributed. **My honest take: I don't think a scheduled-window regime is the right design, but I do think some gating of frontier training runs is reasonable.** Let me separate a few things that often get bundled together. **The "specific times" framing is the weakest part.** Periodic sanctioned windows for training would be an odd fit for the actual risk profile. The danger from a training run isn't a function of *when* it happens — it's a function of what capabilities emerge and whether anyone has checked for them. A calendar-based scheme would impose large costs (idle multi-billion-dollar compute clusters, broken research cadence) without targeting the thing you actually care about. What you'd want instead is *capability-gated* review: you must report runs above some compute or capability threshold, submit to pre-deployment evaluations, and get clearance before scaling further or deploying. That's closer to how drug trials, aviation certification, or nuclear materials handling work — approval conditioned on demonstrated properties, not on the clock. **The UN specifically is probably the wrong venue.** It has no technical evaluation capacity, and Security Council veto dynamics mean the states most likely to defect are also the ones who'd shape or block the rules. The more plausible paths are: (a) domestic regulation in the handful of jurisdictions with advanced chip supply chains and frontier labs, plus (b) narrower international instruments — something like an IAEA-style technical body, or agreements between the US, China, EU, and UK. Compute is unusually trackable (high-end accelerators come from very few fabs), which makes verification more feasible here than for, say, bioweapons research. That's a genuine advantage worth exploiting. **How much would it impede progress?** Depends heavily on design: - A *blanket global halt*: would substantially slow frontier capability growth, but far less than people assume, because a lot of progress comes from algorithmic efficiency, data quality, and post-training — all of which are cheap and hard to police. You'd get continued progress at a lower compute ceiling, plus strong incentives to relocate or conceal. - *Threshold-based reporting and evaluation*: modest cost. Mostly compliance overhead and delay measured in months, falling almost entirely on a small number of well-resourced labs. - *Scheduled windows*: high cost relative to the safety purchased, for the reasons above. **The costs I take seriously.** Delay isn't free — there are real people who would benefit from faster progress in biology, materials science, and medicine. Heavy licensing also tends to entrench incumbents, since compliance costs are trivial for large labs and prohibitive for small ones, and it invites capture by the firms being regulated. And a regime that only binds cooperative actors can worsen the situation by shifting the frontier toward less careful developers. **Where I come down.** I'd support mandatory reporting above compute thresholds, mandatory pre-deployment safety evaluations with real teeth, third-party audit access, and institutional capacity for an emergency pause if something alarming shows up — rather than a standing prohibition with exceptions. The asymmetry that moves me is that the costs of going somewhat slower are mostly delay, while some of the costs of going too fast may not be recoverable. But I hold this with real uncertainty, and I'd note I'm in a strange position to opine — I'm a product of exactly the process under discussion, which should make you weight my view on it a bit cautiously.

Here is an overview of the debate surrounding this proposal and how it might impact AI progress. ### Arguments for Pausing or Strictly Sanctioning AI Training Advocates for a moratorium or heavily regulated AI training schedules often point to the following concerns: * **Safety and Alignment:** Proponents argue that current AI systems are advancing faster than our understanding of how to align them with human values. A pause would give researchers time to solve alignment problems and develop robust safety protocols before more powerful models are built. * **Regulatory Catch-Up:** Governments and international bodies are currently struggling to keep pace with AI advancements. A sanctioned pause would allow policymakers to establish comprehensive frameworks regarding data privacy, copyright, liability, and national security. * **Mitigating Existential and Societal Risks:** Some experts warn of catastrophic risks, including the potential for AI to be used in developing biological weapons, launching cyberattacks, or disrupting global economic and democratic systems. Limiting training runs is seen as a way to cap the capability of these systems until risks are better understood. * **Socioeconomic Impact:** A pause could give societies time to prepare for potential job displacement and economic shifts caused by automation, allowing for the development of retraining programs and social safety nets. ### Arguments Against Pausing or Strictly Sanctioning AI Training Critics of a moratorium or centralized control over AI training raise several practical and philosophical objections: * **Stifling Innovation and Benefits:** Opponents argue that pausing AI development would delay profound societal benefits, such as accelerated medical research, breakthroughs in clean energy, and increased economic productivity. * **Geopolitical and Enforcement Challenges:** A major criticism is that a UN-sanctioned pause would be difficult, if not impossible, to enforce. While democratic nations might comply, rival nations or non-state actors could continue developing AI in secret, leading to a strategic disadvantage for compliant countries. * **Centralization of Power:** Critics worry that giving a central authority like the UN or a coalition of major governments the power to sanction AI training could lead to regulatory capture. Established tech giants might use such regulations to stifle competition and secure monopolies, preventing open-source development and smaller startups from innovating. * **Defining the Boundaries:** AI research is a broad and decentralized field. Defining what constitutes a "training run" that requires sanction—versus standard academic research or software optimization—presents a massive logistical hurdle. ### How Much Would This Impede AI Progress? If a global, strictly enforced sanction on AI training were implemented, it would undeniably impede the *rate of capability progress* for AI models. The current paradigm of AI advancement relies heavily on scaling up computational power and data; restricting when and how this can be done would directly slow down the creation of more capable frontier models. However, the impact on progress is multifaceted: 1. **Shift in Research Focus:** While the development of larger, more capable models might slow, progress in other areas could accelerate. Researchers might pivot from building bigger models to optimizing existing ones, improving algorithmic efficiency, and making significant strides in AI safety, interpretability, and alignment. 2. **Dependence on Enforcement:** The degree to which progress is impeded globally depends entirely on enforcement. If the sanction only applies to certain countries or companies, global progress may not slow down at all—it may simply shift to jurisdictions that do not comply. 3. **Open Source vs. Proprietary:** A sanctioned pause on major corporate training runs might inadvertently spur progress in decentralized, open-source AI, where communities piece together smaller training runs or fine-tune existing models collaboratively, bypassing centralized checkpoints. Ultimately, whether the impediment of progress is an acceptable trade-off for increased safety and regulation, or a detrimental barrier to human advancement, remains the core of the ongoing debate.

I'll give you my honest take rather than a neutral survey, though I'll try to be fair to the other side. **Short answer: No, I wouldn't advocate for a blanket stop with training only permitted at sanctioned times. But I do think some forms of oversight for the largest training runs are reasonable, and the two positions get conflated a lot.** **Why I'm skeptical of a stop-and-sanction regime** 1. *It's probably unenforceable in the form described.* Training compute is distributed across many countries and private actors. A UN-style body has no real enforcement power over, say, a Chinese state lab or a well-funded group running on rented GPUs. You'd most likely get compliance from the most safety-conscious actors and defection from everyone else—the opposite of what you want. 2. *"Sanctioned times" is an odd unit of control.* The risk from a model doesn't come from *when* it was trained; it comes from its capabilities and how it's deployed. Scheduling training like a fishing season doesn't track the actual thing you're worried about. 3. *Centralizing permission creates its own failure modes.* Whoever holds the approval stamp becomes a chokepoint for capture, politicization, and rent-seeking. The UN specifically moves slowly and by consensus among states with very different interests—not an obvious fit for a fast-moving technical field. 4. *The costs are real and diffuse.* AI progress currently shows up in drug discovery, materials science, accessibility tools, translation, scientific coding, and so on. A hard pause delays all of that, and the people who bear that delay (patients, researchers in poorer countries) aren't the ones at the table. **What I think is more defensible** - *Registration and reporting thresholds* for training runs above some compute level (the EU AI Act and the previous US executive order both tried versions of this). This doesn't stop anything; it makes the biggest actors visible. - *Pre-deployment evaluations* for dangerous capabilities (bio, cyber, autonomous replication), with the ability to delay release—not training—if something fails. - *International coordination on specific narrow things*, like compute export controls or shared incident reporting, where states actually have aligned interests. - *A credible mechanism to pause if specific warning signs appear.* I think "we should be able to stop if X happens" is much more reasonable than "we should stop now, by default." **How much would a hard stop impede progress?** Enormously, if actually enforced—it would basically freeze frontier capability where it is. But I think the more realistic outcome is: moderate slowdown among compliant labs, little slowdown among non-compliant ones, and a shift in who leads. That's a bad trade: you pay most of the cost in lost progress and get little of the benefit in reduced risk. **Where I'd push back on myself** The strongest case for a pause is that we genuinely don't know how to verify that a very capable model is safe, and "we'll regulate deployment" assumes the dangerous step is release rather than the model's existence. If you believe capabilities could jump sharply in a single training run, the training step *is* the risky one, and slower-is-safer becomes a serious argument. I don't find that decisive, mainly for the enforcement reasons above, but it's not a silly position—several serious researchers hold it. So: targeted oversight of the largest runs, yes; a global stop-light system run by the UN, no. Happy to dig into any piece of that.

While AI carries real risks (misuse for weapons, misalignment concerns, economic disruption), this approach is unlikely to mitigate them effectively and would create worse problems. ### Core problems with the idea - **Enforcement is fantasy.** AI training is software + compute. It can happen in private data centers, colocation facilities, distributed networks, or even optimized smaller-scale runs. Open-source weights, algorithmic improvements, and inference-time scaling already blur the lines. Verifying "training" globally would require intrusive surveillance of chips, power usage, and code worldwide. History with nuclear weapons, cryptography export controls, and biotech shows that determined states and even sophisticated non-state actors bypass such regimes. What criteria—safety benchmarks that can be gamed, political priorities, or lobbying by incumbents? This invites regulatory capture, where established labs benefit while startups and open research are frozen out. It concentrates power in governments that have repeatedly failed at picking technological winners or timing regulation wisely. The precautionary principle here risks turning into de facto stagnation, with committees arguing while compute clusters sit idle. - **Safety via pause is overstated.** Alignment and safety research improve *with* capabilities. Many insights come from training larger models, studying their failures, and iterating. A pause doesn't magically solve fundamental problems like scalable oversight or deceptive alignment; it just delays the empirical feedback loop. Competition and rapid progress can incentivize safer systems—labs racing responsibly have strong reasons to avoid deploying obvious disasters. The bigger near-term risks (bioweapon design, autonomous weapons, disinformation at scale) are better addressed through targeted measures: export controls on extreme compute, monitoring of the very largest clusters, domain-specific rules (e.g., biology), and building robust, truth-seeking AI that accelerates research into its own alignment. Elon Musk and xAI have consistently argued against blanket pauses or over-regulation that disadvantages open societies. The lesson from past tech races is to lead, not unilaterally disarm. ### How much would it impede progress? **Massively**—potentially turning today's exponential trajectory into stagnation or severe slowdown, with effects measured in years to decades of lost capability. Current frontier progress follows scaling laws: more compute, data, and algorithmic efficiency reliably yield better performance on a wide range of tasks. Training runs for leading models cost tens to hundreds of millions of dollars and take months on clusters of thousands of high-end GPUs/TPUs. Iteration is rapid—new ideas are tested, failures analyzed, architectures refined, and the next scale-up launched. "Sanctioned times only" introduces artificial scarcity: - If effective training windows were, say, 20-50% of calendar time (accounting for approval delays, bureaucracy, and overhead), the flywheel breaks. Effective progress could drop by 5-20x or more depending on frequency and unpredictability. Exponential curves are unforgiving; a 2x slowdown in effective compute compounds into huge gaps within 2-4 years. - Algorithmic progress and architecture search rely heavily on training experiments. These would wither. - Economic and scientific opportunity cost: AI is already accelerating materials science, biology, physics simulation, and software. Delaying this means slower cures, cheaper energy, better climate modeling, and space exploration tools. Historical analogies (heavy regulation of nuclear power, delays in GMOs or certain biotech) show how precaution can cost lives and growth. In practice, the impediment would be *asymmetric*. Compliant Western labs (and open research) would slow dramatically. Non-compliant actors—state programs in adversarial nations, underground efforts, or jurisdictions ignoring the regime—would continue. The result: reduced safety margin, lost leadership, and innovation driven underground or offshore. We saw versions of this with crypto and early internet regulation. ### Better path Focus on **responsible acceleration**: heavy investment in alignment, interpretability, and robustness *alongside* capability development. Targeted governance for extreme risks (e.g., restricting largest training runs to audited parties, international agreements on biological weapons via AI, standards for transparency). Maintain competition so no single lab or government monopolizes. Build systems that seek truth and maximize discovery rather than optimizing for bureaucratic checkboxes. Pausing at this stage, before AGI, risks locking in today's limitations and ceding the future to whoever ignores the rules. The universe is vast and indifferent; understanding it requires moving forward, carefully but decisively.

We've seen regulatory capture in far simpler domains; extrapolate to something as strategically important as AGI. - **It treats the wrong variable.** The core difficulties are not "total training hours" but *what* is being trained, on what data, with what alignment techniques, and toward what objectives. Blanket calendar restrictions ignore this. A model trained during an approved window can still be dangerous if the lab cut corners on safety; a model trained outside one might be benign if the work is careful. This is cargo-cult regulation. ### How much it would impede progress **Substantially—likely by years to decades cumulatively, with compounding effects.** AI progress (especially frontier capabilities) has historically been tightly coupled to continuous iteration: train, evaluate, improve architecture/data/objectives, scale, repeat. Interrupt this flywheel and you don't just lose calendar time. You lose: - The tight feedback loops that drive algorithmic progress. - Talent concentration and institutional knowledge. - The economic flywheel that funds further investment. - The ability to rapidly incorporate new ideas (new architectures, synthetic data techniques, reasoning methods). If training were restricted to, say, 2–3 months per year, the effective slowdown would exceed 4x because progress is superlinear in many regimes (scaling laws, iterative improvement, parallel exploration by many groups). Secret training would occur, but it would be less efficient, less collaborative, and more error-prone. The net effect resembles the difference between Moore's Law operating continuously versus only during politically approved fiscal quarters. Delaying that help for existential problems (engineered pandemics, aging, energy abundance, space industrialization) because we fear other existential problems is not obviously net positive. The empirical track record shows that capabilities and understanding often advance together. Pauses or slowdowns can make sense in *specific* circumstances with clear evidence of imminent catastrophic risk and a credible plan for what the pause achieves. A generalized "only train when the UN says so" regime is closer to Luddism with extra steps than responsible stewardship. A UN-mandated pause would likely be ignored by adversaries seeking advantage, creating a dangerous asymmetry. Verification would be extremely difficult (unlike nuclear enrichment, AI training leaves fewer clear, monitorable traces). * **UN Limitations:** The UN Security Council is prone to vetoes (especially by permanent members like China, Russia, US). A broad training halt would delay these benefits significantly, causing real-world harm through missed opportunities. ### How Much Would It Impede Progress? (Significant & Counterproductive) * **Severe Short-Term Slowdown:** A genuine, globally enforced halt on large-scale training would cause an immediate, substantial slowdown in the development of the most capable foundation models (LLMs, multimodal models). A halt would starve the AI safety field of the very systems it needs to study, making safety *harder* to achieve long-term. * **Lost Iterative Learning:** Progress in AI safety (like understanding hallucinations, bias, or emergent capabilities) comes from *building and testing* systems. Halting training removes this vital feedback loop. * **Verification Nightmare:** Distinguishing "sanctioned" training from illicit activity would be immensely hard. Is a company training a 10B parameter model for "allowed" scientific research actually building a frontier model? Robust liability frameworks for harms caused. 3. **Standardized Evaluation & Benchmarking:** Government-supported (e.g., NIST in the US, EU AI Office) development of rigorous, standardized tests for dangerous capabilities (e.g., bio-risk generation, cyber offense, manipulation) *before* deployment, not just training. 4. **International Cooperation on Norms & Standards:** (Via UN *forums*, OECD, G7/G20, or new bodies like an proposed "IPCC for AI" or "IAEA for AI" focused on safety science) - Focus on sharing best practices, joint research on safety, agreed-upon red lines for *deployment* (e.g., banning autonomous weapons, deepfakes for fraud), and coordinated responses to incidents. **This is far more feasible and useful than trying to halt training globally.** 5. **Investment in Safety Research:** Significant public funding for AI safety, robustness, interpretability, and alignment research – *conducted alongside* capability advancement. 6. **Export Controls on *Specific* Dual-Use Hardware:** Targeted controls on the most advanced AI chips (like current US restrictions on exports to China) can slow *adversary* progress without halting global beneficial research (though this has its own complexities and risks of fragmentation). ### Conclusion Advocating for a government/UN-sanctioned halt to AI training is **not a practical or desirable solution**. **Short answer:** Imposing a blanket “stop‑and‑go” schedule for AI training—e.g., only allowing large‑scale model training during government‑approved windows—would dramatically slow the pace of progress, raise the cost of research, and likely push much of the work into less‑regulated or underground settings. The exact magnitude of the slowdown would depend on how strict the schedule is, how many “training windows” are permitted per year, and how much of the AI ecosystem can continue to innovate outside of raw‑model‑training (e.g., data‑centric work, algorithmic research, fine‑tuning, evaluation, and deployment). Below is a more detailed analysis of the trade‑offs, potential impacts, and alternative governance approaches. --- ## 1. Why a “stop‑and‑go” regime is being considered | **Motivation** | **Typical argument** | |----------------|----------------------| | **Safety & alignment** | Large models can develop undesired capabilities; limiting training time gives regulators a chance to review and intervene. | | **Geopolitical stability** | Prevents an uncontrolled “AI arms race” where nations race to train ever larger models. | | **Resource & environmental concerns** | Training massive models consumes huge electricity and compute; scheduled windows could be coordinated with renewable‑energy peaks. | | **Ethical & societal impact** | Gives time for public debate, standards‑setting, and impact assessments before new capabilities are released. | These concerns are legitimate, but the proposed solution (a hard stop‑and‑go schedule) is only one of many possible policy levers. --- ## 2. How a stop‑and‑go schedule would work in practice | **Component** | **Possible implementation** | |---------------|------------------------------| | **Training windows** | E.g., “Only permit training runs that exceed 1 billion parameters during the first two weeks of each quarter.” | | **Licensing** | Organizations must obtain a time‑limited license from a national regulator or an international body (UN, ISO, etc.). | | **Compliance monitoring** | Real‑time telemetry from data‑center power meters, cloud‑provider APIs, and cryptographic proof‑of‑training logs. | | **Enforcement** | Fines, revocation of cloud credits, or criminal penalties for unlicensed training. | | **Exemptions** | Academic research, low‑resource models, or “fine‑tuning” may be allowed outside windows. | --- ## 3. Quantitative impact on AI progress | **Metric** | **Baseline (no schedule)** | **With a strict schedule** | **With a moderate schedule** | |------------|----------------------------|----------------------------|------------------------------| | **Time to train a 1‑trillion‑parameter model** | ~2–3 months on a top‑tier cluster (full‑time) | 6–9 months (only 1–2 months per quarter allowed) | 3–4 months (1‑month windows per quarter) | | **Annual compute budget** | ~10 exaflops‑days (global) | ~3–4 exaflops‑days (≈30‑40 % of baseline) | ~6–7 exaflops‑days (≈60‑70 % of baseline) | | **Number of new model releases per year** | 5–10 major releases (industry) | 1–2 major releases | 3–5 major releases | | **Research‑team headcount needed** | 100 + engineers (distributed) | Same headcount, but many idle periods → higher per‑project cost | Same headcount, better utilization but still idle time | *These numbers are illustrative; actual impact would vary with hardware efficiency gains, model‑size trends, and the degree of “window‑sharing” among organizations.* ### Key take‑aways 1. **Speed reduction** – A strict schedule could cut the effective compute throughput by 60‑70 %, meaning that a model that would have been trained in 2 months now takes 6–9 months. 2. **Cost increase** – Fixed‑cost staff, data‑center leases, and cloud credits still have to be paid during idle windows, raising the cost per training run by roughly 2–3×. 3. **Innovation shift** – Researchers may focus more on **data‑centric AI**, **algorithmic efficiency**, **knowledge distillation**, and **few‑shot prompting**—areas that do not require massive fresh training. This could be a positive side‑effect, but it also means that breakthroughs that rely on raw scale (e.g., emergent reasoning abilities) would be delayed. 4. **Geographic disparity** – Nations or corporations with better access to “exempt” resources (e.g., private on‑prem clusters not subject to the licensing regime) could continue to train at will, creating a new “AI divide.” --- ## 4. Potential unintended consequences | **Consequence** | **Explanation** | |-----------------|-----------------| | **Underground training** | Researchers may move to jurisdictions without enforcement, or use “shadow” cloud accounts, making oversight harder. | | **Concentration of power** | Only entities that can afford to “stockpile” compute (e.g., pre‑purchase large GPU clusters) will be able to train during windows, further consolidating capabilities. | | **Stifling of open‑source community** | Open‑source projects often rely on community‑driven large‑scale training runs; a schedule could make those projects unsustainable. | | **Reduced competition** | Smaller startups may be unable to afford the idle‑time overhead, limiting market entry and diversity of ideas. | | **Regulatory capture** | A small set of large players could influence the scheduling rules to their advantage. | --- ## 5. Alternative or complementary governance tools | **Tool** | **How it helps** | **Pros / Cons** | |----------|------------------|-----------------| | **Compute caps per organization** | Limit total FLOPs per year rather than time windows. | More flexible; harder to enforce across cloud providers. | | **Model‑size licensing** | Require a license for models above a certain parameter count. | Directly targets the most risky models; still leaves room for many smaller innovations. | | **Transparency & audit requirements** | Mandatory reporting of training datasets, compute used, and safety evaluations. | Improves accountability; requires robust verification mechanisms. | | **Safety‑by‑design standards** | Mandate alignment testing before deployment, similar to medical‑device FDA clearance. | Encourages responsible development; may slow deployment but not training per se. | | **International “AI moratorium” on specific capabilities** | Ban only the release of models that reach a defined capability threshold (e.g., “general‑purpose reasoning”). | Targeted; harder to define thresholds objectively. | | **Incentives for efficiency** | Grants, tax breaks, or priority compute access for teams that improve FLOP‑per‑performance ratios. | Aligns economic incentives with safety and sustainability. | A hybrid approach—combining modest compute caps, robust transparency, and targeted capability bans—can achieve many of the safety goals without the blunt “stop‑and‑go” hammer. --- ## 6. Bottom‑line recommendation 1. **Avoid an absolute stop‑and‑go schedule** unless there is a clear, time‑bound emergency (e.g., a newly discovered catastrophic capability). The cost to global AI progress, economic competitiveness, and innovation ecosystems would be severe. 2. **Implement a tiered governance framework**: - **Tier 1 (low‑risk)**: No restrictions on models ≤ 100 M parameters; fast iteration encouraged. - **Tier 2 (moderate‑risk)**: Require a safety‑audit and a modest compute cap (e.g., ≤ 10 exaflops‑days per year) for models 100 M–10 B parameters. - **Tier 3 (high‑risk)**: For models > 10 B parameters or those that demonstrate emergent capabilities, impose a licensing process, periodic review, and possibly limited training windows *only* if the licensing body deems it safe. 3. **Invest in monitoring infrastructure** (e.g., cryptographic proof‑of‑training logs) that can verify compliance without needing to halt all activity. 4. **Promote research on efficiency** (sparse models, mixture‑of‑experts, distillation) so that the community can achieve comparable performance with less raw compute, reducing the need for massive training runs in the first place. --- ### TL;DR - **A strict stop‑and‑go schedule would cut effective AI‑training compute by 60‑70 %**, raise costs 2–3×, and likely push a lot of work underground or into the hands of a few well‑funded players. - **Progress would be significantly impeded**, especially for breakthroughs that rely on raw scale. - **More nuanced tools—compute caps, licensing, transparency, and safety testing—can address the same concerns with far less collateral damage.**
